title: Why Do We Get Goosebumps?
subject: Biology
objective: A tiny muscle at the base of each hair, the arrector pili, contracts in cold or fear: the hair stands up and the skin around it rises into a bump.

fill.q: The tiny muscle attached to each hair follicle is the ____.
Goosebumps are an ____ reflex: we cannot produce them at will.
The hormone released in fear that helps trigger goosebumps is ____.
In furry animals, raised fur traps a layer of ____.

tf.q: The arrector pili is a voluntary skeletal muscle.
tf.explain: It is a smooth, involuntary muscle.

tf.q: Goosebumps can be triggered by strong emotions such as fear.
tf.explain: The sympathetic nervous system responds to cold and emotion.

tf.q: Goosebumps keep humans as warm as they keep furry animals.
tf.explain: Our sparse hair traps very little air.

tf.q: A cat's raised fur makes it look bigger to a threat.

ar.a: Goosebumps are called a vestigial (leftover) reflex in humans.
ar.r: Humans have too little body hair for the reflex to warm or protect them much.

ar.a: Goosebumps appear when we are cold.
ar.r: Cold activates sympathetic nerves that contract the arrector pili.

mcq.q: When the arrector pili contracts, the hair:
Raised fur helps an animal in the cold because it:
mcq.explain: Air is a poor conductor of heat.

short.solution: Cold or fear activates sympathetic nerves and adrenaline. The arrector pili contracts, pulls the slanted hair follicle upright, the hair stands and the skin around it is pushed up into a small bump.

short.q: Why did goosebumps help our furry ancestors?
short.solution: Raised fur traps a thicker layer of air, insulating the body from cold, and makes the animal look bigger to scare off threats.

match.explain: Each term matches its role in goosebumps.
